q: What is deep learning?
short: Machine learning with neural networks of many layers that learn successively higher-level representations from data.
detail: Representation learning replaces manual feature engineering; trained with gradient descent and backpropagation.
follow: How is it different from classical ML?

q: AI vs ML vs DL?
short: AI: making machines smart (any method). ML: an approach to AI that learns from experience. DL: a technique within ML using deep neural networks.
detail: Nested: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ NN ⊃ DL.
follow: Give an AI system that isn't ML.

q: Why has deep learning become so successful recently?
short: Big (often unstructured) data, cheap compute (GPUs) and storage, better algorithms and software, and the fact that large networks keep improving with data.
detail: Ng's scale curve; scaling laws.

q: Name the four components of a deep learning problem.
short: Data, model, objective (loss) function, learning algorithm.
detail: The algorithm (e.g. gradient descent) adjusts model parameters to minimise the loss on the data.
follow: Why must the loss be differentiable?
mistakes: Confusing the loss with the evaluation metric.

q: What is a loss function?
short: A formal measure of how badly the model does, defined so lower is better.
detail: Squared error for regression, cross-entropy for classification; usually differentiable.

q: What is gradient descent?
short: An iterative algorithm that moves parameters opposite the gradient of the loss: θ ← θ − η∇L.
detail: Variants: stochastic/mini-batch, momentum, Adam.
follow: What does the learning rate control?
mistakes: Moving along the gradient instead of against it.

q: Features vs labels?
short: Features are the input attributes (covariates) of an example; the label (target) is what we predict in supervised learning.
detail: D = {X, t}; N examples, d features.
mistakes: Including the target among the features.

q: Supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning?
short: Supervised: labelled examples; unsupervised: features only (structure, density, generation); reinforcement: an agent learns from rewards by acting in an environment.
detail: Self-supervised learning creates labels from the data.

q: Multi-class vs multi-label classification?
short: Multi-class: exactly one of K classes (softmax). Multi-label: any subset of labels (independent sigmoids).
detail: Losses: categorical vs per-label binary cross-entropy.

q: Which network type suits which input?
short: Tabular → standard (fully connected) NN; images → CNN; sequences (audio, text) → RNN/Transformer; multiple sensors → hybrid.
detail: From the application table.

q: Why does depth require non-linear activations?
short: A composition of linear layers is linear: W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ = W'x + b'. Non-linearities let depth build richer functions.
detail: ReLU, tanh, sigmoid (Module 5).
example: Linear model 52% vs 1 hidden layer 99.5% on rings.
follow: What is the universal approximation theorem?
mistakes: Stacking linear layers and expecting more power.

q: What is a 'family of models'?
short: The set of input–output mappings obtainable by varying the parameters of a fixed architecture (the hypothesis space).
detail: Choosing the architecture chooses the family; training picks a member.
example: One wake-word architecture for 'Alexa' and 'Hey Siri'.
follow: How does family size relate to overfitting?
mistakes: Confusing the trained model with the family.

q: What does 'representation learning' mean?
short: Learning useful intermediate features automatically from raw data rather than hand-designing them.
detail: Each hidden layer is a learned representation; later layers become task-specific.
follow: How do you inspect learned representations?

q: You have 500 rows of tabular data. Deep learning or gradient boosting?
short: Usually gradient boosting or a regularised linear model: small tabular data favours classical methods; DL needs more data or strong priors.
detail: Try both with cross-validation.

q: Why standardise inputs before gradient descent?
short: Features on very different scales make the loss surface elongated, so one learning rate is too large for some directions and too small for others.
detail: Standardising rounds the surface and speeds convergence.

q: How are sequence-learning tasks different from standard classification?
short: Inputs and/or outputs are variable-length sequences with order dependence (tagging, ASR, TTS, translation).
detail: Need architectures that share parameters over time (RNNs, Transformers).

q: What does the model estimate in supervised learning?
short: The conditional distribution P(label | features) (or a point prediction derived from it).
detail: Cross-entropy training = maximum likelihood of that distribution.
follow: How does this relate to MLE?

q: Your training loss falls but validation loss rises. What's happening?
short: Overfitting: the model memorises training data.
detail: Add data/augmentation, regularisation (weight decay, dropout), early stopping, smaller model (Module 11).
follow: How do you choose the stopping point?

q: What are neural scaling laws?
short: Empirical power laws: test loss falls predictably as a power of data, parameters and compute when the others aren't bottlenecks.
detail: Used to plan compute-optimal model sizes (Chinchilla: ~20 tokens per parameter).
example: Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022.

q: Why is the neural-network loss non-convex, and why does training still work?
short: Hidden-unit permutation symmetry and non-linearities create many minima and saddles; in high dimensions most critical points are saddles and many minima generalise similarly.
detail: SGD noise helps escape saddles; overparameterisation smooths the landscape.
example: Training deep nets reliably from random init.
mistakes: Claiming GD finds the global minimum.

q: Discriminative vs generative deep models?
short: Discriminative models learn P(y | x) (classifiers); generative models learn P(x) or P(x, y) and can sample (GANs, VAEs, diffusion, LLMs).
detail: Generative pre-training often yields good representations for discriminative tasks.

q: How does self-supervised learning fit the taxonomy?
short: It uses unlabelled data but creates supervised targets from the data itself (masking, next-token prediction, contrastive pairs).
detail: Bridges unsupervised and supervised; basis of foundation models.

q: You must build a wake-word detector for a phone. Walk through the framework.
short: Define input (1 s audio frames → spectrogram) and output (yes/no); collect and label many positive/negative clips across speakers and noise; choose a small CNN/RNN family; loss = binary cross-entropy; train with SGD/Adam; evaluate false-accept/false-reject rates on held-out speakers; optimise for on-device latency.
detail: Class imbalance: wake word is rare.
mistakes: Evaluating on speakers seen in training.

q: What is the role of the learning algorithm vs the model?
short: The model defines the family of functions; the algorithm searches it for parameters minimising the loss. Different algorithms (SGD, Adam) can reach different solutions with different generalisation.
detail: Implicit bias of SGD toward flat minima.
example: Adam vs SGD on image classification.
mistakes: Thinking the optimiser doesn't affect the final model.
